title: Software Engineering Techniques
subtitle: Objects, project structure, testing and simple AI pipelines.
scenario: A smart classroom combines temperature sensors, a trained classifier and an information display.
sections: From one long script to several components
A monitoring program now contains sensor code, decisions and screen output.
Break a program into parts with clear responsibilities. Object-oriented programming is one way to organise related data and behaviour.
A Sensor supplies a measurement; a Controller decides an action; a Dashboard displays it.
The same app reads from several temperature sensors.
A class describes a type of object; an instance stores its own state and exposes methods. Keep examples small and practical.
Two Sensor objects can each have a different current value.

class Sensor:
    def __init__(self,value):self.value=value
    def read(self):return self.value
print(Sensor(17).read(), Sensor(21).read())
A classifier receives poorly formatted measurements.
An AI application has stages: collect → clean → predict → decide → display → test. Each stage should be testable independently.
Bad data should be rejected before a classifier makes an unreliable prediction.
Record the output and any warning
Two students edit the same application at different times.
Versions track changes; Git commits store meaningful snapshots, while branches and pull requests support review. GitHub is optional for students without accounts.
'Add missing-data warning' is more informative than 'update'.
print('Commit message: Handle missing sensor readings')

title: FIICode I: Understanding the Challenge
subtitle: Read the specification, examine the data and plan a real hackathon project.
scenario: A small team receives a dataset and must propose a genuinely useful AI-powered tool.
sections: Turn a problem into inputs and outputs
A challenge says 'help students choose study sessions'.
Translate a story into a precise deliverable: what data do we have, what decision is expected, and how will success be measured?
Input: student availability and preferences; output: a recommended timetable.
A file has duplicate rows, missing values and unclear units.
Use a small data dictionary and simple plots to understand a dataset before selecting an algorithm.
Ten records with two missing labels do not give ten labelled training examples.

rows=[{'label':'A'},{'label':None}]
print(sum(r['label'] is None for r in rows))
The team is tempted to start with a neural network.
A baseline is a small system that already works and can be measured. It may be a rule, a most-frequent-class prediction, or a simple tree.
If 7/10 training labels are 'yes', always guessing 'yes' is a baseline; it may be inadequate but it sets a comparison point.

lab.context: Team-based FIICode project: a clear problem, a reproducible dataset and an initial baseline.
steps: Read the exact challenge rules and identify allowed inputs.
Inspect a small CSV without changing the provided answer column.
Choose a baseline and run it on held-out examples.
Write down the model's first score and one weakness.
lab.research: Compare two possible baselines and justify which is easier to maintain.

homework.mandatory: Write a one-paragraph problem statement and a data dictionary.
homework.homework: Deliver a runnable baseline notebook with a metric and a description of its input/output.

advanced: Find a hidden assumption in a competition statement.
Design a fair validation plan without using hidden test answers.

title: FIICode II: Implementing the Application
subtitle: Make the data pipeline, model and interface work together.
scenario: A hackathon project predicts a category but has no usable application yet.
sections: The model works in a notebook but nobody can interact with it.
Build the smallest complete path from input to useful output before adding features.
One CSV row → one prediction → a clear label on screen is a valid starting demo.

def predict(value):return 'high' if value>20 else 'normal'
print(predict(23))
Data cleaning and user-interface code are mixed together.
Keep input validation, prediction and display in small testable functions or classes. OOP can help but is not mandatory.
If the input is missing, return an understandable error instead of a stack trace.
A demo crashes if someone enters a blank value.
Write tests for normal inputs, boundary values and missing data. Testing is cheaper than explaining a crash during a presentation.
Try values below, equal to, and above a decision threshold.

lab.context: Turn the Week 12 baseline into an end-to-end interactive demonstration.
steps: Load an example input and validate its fields.
Connect the prepared model to a simple interface.
Test the main success path and one error path.
Save a working version before extending anything else.
lab.research: Design a second output format, for example a report CSV with an explanation.

homework.context: Judges need to try a prototype without learning how its internal notebook is organised.
homework.mandatory: Expose a simple input and readable prediction.
homework.homework: Add one validation rule and three small tests.

title: FIICode III: Improving and Testing
subtitle: Improve one thing at a time, using actual measurements.
scenario: A prototype works for most test inputs but fails on some important cases.
sections: An app gets seven of ten categories right.
An average score does not identify which errors matter; inspect mistakes by input type and class.
If all three failures occur on night-time readings, investigate that feature before changing the entire model.

actual=['A','A','B','B']; pred=['A','B','B','B']
print(sum(a==b for a,b in zip(actual,pred)))
Two students independently change parameters and features.
Change one factor at a time and compare results on the same validation data. Avoid choosing a model based on final hidden test answers.
Baseline: 0.70; one feature added: 0.75; check whether improvement repeats.
The project works only on the author's computer.
Keep a reproducible environment, sample inputs and clear steps. Handle missing data and explain limitations.
A README should let another student run the same notebook and understand the outputs.
print('README: inputs, how to run, known limitations')

title: FIICode IV: Hackathon
subtitle: A real challenge, a functioning application and an evidence-based presentation.
scenario: Your team must present a working solution, not just a model trained once.
sections: A working project still has unfinished features.
Choose the tasks that make the demo reliable and understandable. Avoid major untested rewrites near presentation.
Prioritise 'runs on a fresh browser' before 'add five new model types'.
A judge asks what improved and how the team knows.
Show the problem, baseline, method, validation metric, a real example and one limitation. A demonstration is an argument supported by observable outputs.
'Accuracy improved from 70% to 78% on the same 50 held-out examples' is stronger than 'our AI is very accurate'.
Deliver something someone else can run
The team members want to reuse the project later.
Package source code or notebooks, a small example dataset, usage instructions and a short changelog. Protect private data.
A clean project can be restarted and reproduced by someone who did not write it.
print('Deliver: code, README, sample data, result summary')
